1	# Entire Continuity
2	
3	## One-sentence summary
4	
5	Entire Continuity makes autonomous software work resumable: it turns fragmented agent sessions
6	into a Git-linked, evidence-backed engineering task state that another agent or a human can
7	verify and continue.
8	
9	**The agent changes. The task doesn't.**
10	
11	---
12	
13	## Problem, intended user and why it matters
14	
15	When a software task moves between agents, sub-agents, scheduled sessions or humans, the next
16	worker has to reconstruct the engineering state from fragments. Git shows what the code *is*. It
17	does not show what was intended, what was already tried and abandoned, which requirement is still
18	open, which test is failing, or why the obvious approach was rejected.
19	
20	So the next worker re-investigates, re-derives, and — the expensive failure — **repeats an
21	approach the previous worker already proved doesn't work**, because a fresh session has no memory
22	of the failure and the repository does not record it.
23	
24	The intended user is a developer running agents that work asynchronously and in parallel: an
25	OpenClaw main session delegating to coding and test sub-agents, a Hermes continuation, a human
26	picking it up on Monday. The unit that has to survive all of them is not the session. It is the
27	**task**.
28	
29	What this deliberately is *not*: a generic agent-memory product. A memory product answers "what
30	did the model remember?" This answers **"what is the current engineering state of this task, what
31	evidence supports it, and what should the next worker do?"**
32	
33	---
34	
35	## Selected Entire track and why Entire is essential
36	
37	**Track T3 — Bring Entire to a New Agent or Workflow.**
38	
39	Entire is the authoritative development-history layer, and this project deliberately does not
40	compete with it. The architecture is:
41	
42	```
43	agent execution → Entire session/checkpoint → task-state interpretation → human/agent continuity
44	```
45	
46	and explicitly *not*:
47	
48	```
49	agent execution → a new independent database → Entire becomes optional
50	```
51	
52	Checkpoints are the substrate. A checkpoint already ties development context to Git history; this
53	project reads that and turns it into a structured engineering state with evidence attached, then
54	hands it to the next worker. Without a history layer there is nothing to continue *from* — the
55	system would be reduced to summarising a transcript, which is exactly the thing the plan rules
56	out.
57	
58	---
59	
60	## Architecture and main workflow
61	
62	```
63	   OpenClaw ──┐
64	   Hermes ────┼──▶  Normalized Agent Event Model  ──▶  Task State Engine  ──▶  Entire
65	   AcmeCode ──┘         (one vocabulary)              (evidence + merge)      (checkpoints)
66	                                                              │
67	                                                              ▼
68	                                          ┌───────────────────┴──────────────────┐
69	                                          ▼                                      ▼
70	                                    Markdown / text                            JSON
71	                                        human                                  agent
72	```
73	
74	Both outputs render from **one** `EngineeringState` object. Human and machine handoffs are never
75	implemented separately — that is what keeps them consistent.
76	
77	Two rules govern every layer, and they are correctness requirements rather than style:
78	
79	1. **Evidence.** Every semantic claim points at a concrete artifact — a commit, a file and line
80	   range, a test result, a checkpoint. `model.ConfidenceFor` is the single chokepoint: a claim
81	   with no evidence can never be better than `UNKNOWN`, and one backed only by inference can never
82	   be `OBSERVED`.
83	2. **Honesty about gaps.** Every state carries a `Capture` block recording which inputs were
84	   actually available. When anything is missing the output prints a `STATE PARTIALLY RECOVERED`
85	   block naming exactly what is unverified. `validate.Enforce` is monotonically downgrading by
86	   construction — it can weaken a claim, never strengthen one.
87	
88	### Packages
89	
90	| Package | Responsibility |
91	|---|---|
92	| `internal/model` | Frozen domain contract: events, task identity, engineering state, evidence, ports |
93	| `internal/normalize` | Three transcript formats → one event vocabulary, with per-record format detection |
94	| `internal/redact` | Credentials never reach a checkpoint |
95	| `internal/gitrepo` | Level 1 repository facts |
96	| `internal/derive` | Deterministic state — what the system can prove without a model |
97	| `internal/semantic` | Model-assisted extraction (rule-based here), always evidence-attached |
98	| `internal/merge` | The §32 merge rules: failures survive, decisions survive, completion needs evidence |
99	| `internal/validate` | Validation with safe downgrade |
100	| `internal/drift` | Historical state vs the live tree |
101	| `internal/graph` | Graph verification — real Go static analysis when Entire Graph is absent |
102	| `internal/entire` | Checkpoint port, real CLI or local fallback, always says which |
103	| `internal/contextbuild` | The resume pipeline |
104	| `internal/handoff` | Human, Markdown and JSON handoff from one state |
105	| `internal/render` | Every human-facing view |
106	| `internal/e2e` | Acceptance tests against a real git repository |
107	| `examples/billing` | Demo domain (separate module) with one deliberately failing test |
108	
109	### Test layers (plan §63)
110	
111	| Layer | Where |
112	|---|---|
113	| Unit | every `internal/*` package — merge rules, evidence linking, drift, validation, redaction |
114	| Adapter | `internal/normalize` — fixtures per format, plus the real Node shims round-tripped |
115	| Integration | `internal/entire`, `internal/store` — session → checkpoint → task state |
116	| End-to-end | `internal/e2e` — the four acceptance tests below, against a throwaway git repo |
117	
118	The acceptance tests are the ones that assert the product's actual claims:
119	
120	- **`TestFreshSessionRecoversTheTask`** (plan §43) — a session with no chat history recovers the
121	  intent, the failing test, the requirements and, critically, **the approach already rejected**,
122	  so it does not re-derive the broken one.
123	- **`TestRepositoryDriftIsDetected`** (plan §46) — a human commits a change to a file the
124	  checkpoint depends on; the next resume demands revalidation instead of replaying stale claims.
125	- **`TestCrossAgentContinuity`** (plan §44) — one task id, two runtimes, identical intent,
126	  rejected approaches and test state on both sides of the boundary.
127	- **`TestNewFormatFlowsThroughTheWholePipeline`** — the curveball fixture end to end.
128	
129	### Main workflow
130	
131	```bash
132	# a task exists independently of whoever is working on it
133	entire-continuity task init --title "Implement subscription pause" --intent "..."
134	
135	# agent activity flows in from any supported adapter format
136	entire-continuity ingest --file transcript.jsonl
137	
138	# milestone
139	entire-continuity checkpoint create --label "CP2 pre-curveball stable"
140	
141	# ... session ends, agent is gone ...
142	
143	# a fresh worker recovers the task
144	entire-continuity task handoff          # human
145	entire-continuity task resume --json    # agent
146	```
147	
148	`task resume` runs: resolve task → latest checkpoint → historical state → derive current
149	repository truth → merge → validate → **drift detection** → **Graph verification of the next
150	action** → compact continuation context. The receiving agent gets an ordered brief, never a
151	transcript dump, and it is always told: *this is historical context, not authority — verify before
152	you rely on it.*
153	
154	---
155	
156	## Entire Graph findings and verification
157	
158	Full analysis with raw output: **[docs/GRAPH.md](docs/GRAPH.md)**.
159	
160	Graph is used in three places in the actual workflow, not as a compliance step:
161	
162	1. **Definition lookup** — `graph search` / `graph impact` resolve a next-action target to a real
163	   definition with a file and line range.
164	2. **Impact analysis before a high-risk change** — run at *resume* time, before the agent edits,
165	   and again by us before the curveball edit. It reports callers, dependent components and the
166	   tests that exercise them, and produces a *decision*, not a dump.
167	3. **Semantic diff** — exported declaration sets compared across two revisions.
168	
169	The decisive finding: **`model.AgentEvent.Validate` has three callers** (`normalize`, `derive`,
170	`store.FS`). That single fact chose the design. The new transcript format has no task id and names
171	an unknown runtime, so the options were to relax validation — rippling across three packages and
172	weakening the invariant that every stored event is anchored — or to satisfy validation at the
173	decode boundary, touching one. We took the second. Graph is why that is a measured decision rather
174	than a guess.
175	
176	Graph also confirmed `store.AppendEvent` (5 callers) and `entire.CreateCheckpoint` (1 caller) sit
177	*outside* the blast radius, which is what let us assert that checkpoint behaviour stays compatible
178	instead of hoping so.
179	
180	---
181	
182	## Noon Curveball: what changed and how we adapted
183	
184	Full write-up: **[docs/CURVEBALL.md](docs/CURVEBALL.md)**.
185	
186	**Track 3 card: the agent changed its format.** Existing users still produce the original format.
187	
188	### The assumption that was invalidated
189	
190	> *"Each host agent emits exactly one, stable, fully-enumerable lifecycle format. A normalizer is
191	> therefore a total function from raw envelope to known event, and anything it does not recognise
192	> is noise that can be discarded."*
193	
194	It was wrong three ways at once, and the real fixture broke it harder than the card implied:
195	
196	| Assumption | How it broke |
197	|---|---|
198	| One format per agent | `normalize.For(agent)` had no format dimension at all — two formats are live simultaneously |
199	| Unknown records are noise | Silently skipping them makes a short timeline render as a complete one |
200	| A transcript is complete or invalid | One truncated line discarded an entire recoverable session |
201	| *(unpredicted)* The world is enumerable | The fixture carries **no task id** and names a runtime, **AcmeCode**, outside the agent vocabulary — so every one of its events failed validation |
202	
203	### How the design changed
204	
205	- **Format became a dimension**, detected *per record* — so a stream mixing old and new records,
206	  which is what a partially-migrated fleet actually produces, decodes correctly.
207	- **One engine, three mapping tables.** The v1 mappers are reused verbatim; framing, redaction,
208	  validation and lineage folding are shared. The second format added a table, not a pipeline.
209	- **Unknown events are retained**, not dropped — as `model.EventUnknown` carrying the host's own
210	  name in `raw_kind` — and counted in a `Report` that flows into `Capture`.
211	- **Anchoring moved to the decode boundary.** No task id? Derive one from repository + branch +
212	  session via the existing `model.NewTaskID`, which also makes ingestion idempotent.
213	- **The agent vocabulary was widened**, a strict widening that cannot reject anything it accepted
214	  before. Two packages had already built private workarounds for the closed enum; both became
215	  redundant, which is the tell that the defect was in the model.
216	
217	### Why the new result is safe
218	
219	1. **The original format is pinned by comparison, not by hope.** `TestOriginalFormatsStillDecode`
220	   runs the v1 fixtures through *both* the old path and the new one and asserts the events are
221	   byte-identical.
222	2. **The checkpoint path is untouched** — confirmed by Graph caller analysis, not assumed.
223	   `schema_version` is unchanged and no field was repurposed.
224	3. **New information can only make output more cautious.** Unknown and malformed counts only widen
225	   `Capture.Missing`, and `validate.Enforce` cannot strengthen a claim.
226	4. **The failure mode moved in the safe direction**: from *confidently wrong* (a session silently
227	   discarded, rendering clean) to *explicitly incomplete*.
228	
229	---
230	
231	## Checkpoint links and what each checkpoint proves
232	
233	The four required milestones, and the commit that carries each. Development ran in a standalone
234	repository (`Yash-1706/btw-hack`) before the work was relocated into this Entire mirror clone, so
235	the milestone commits below are git-timestamped in that history and land here as the squashed
236	`a7a82fa`:
237	
238	| Milestone | Commit | What it proves |
239	|---|---|---|
240	| **CP1** — Initial understanding and intended architecture | `ebc1da4` | The domain contract frozen before any implementation: evidence model, normalized events, task identity, port interfaces |
241	| **CP2** — Last stable state before the Noon Curveball | `e04266c` | A complete, working v1: engine, CLI, resume and handoff. The state the curveball revision had to preserve |
242	| **CP2.5** — Graph impact analysis, before editing | `2a6250b` | Impact analysis run *before* the change, with the finding that chose the design |
243	| **CP3** — Response to the Noon Curveball | `3f2ffa6` | Both formats supported, unknown events retained, partial transcripts recovered, existing behaviour pinned |
244	| **CP4** — Relocation, real Graph, and the finding it produced | `a7a82fa`, `a58128b`, `dadb65d` | The agent in the designated fork; Entire Graph's closed-set finding, the live defect it exposed, and the test that pins it |
245	
246	**On Entire Checkpoints specifically, stated plainly.** Entire creates checkpoints by capturing an
247	*agent session* through hooks installed in the enabled repository. The engineering work above was
248	performed by an agent session running in the standalone repository, before this mirror clone
249	existed, so those sessions were not captured here and `entire checkpoint list` shows none for them.
250	There is no retroactive checkpoint command, and inventing one would be dishonest.
251	
252	What *is* verifiable: every milestone is a real, timestamped git commit, and the reasoning at each
253	is captured in [docs/CURVEBALL.md](docs/CURVEBALL.md) and [docs/GRAPH.md](docs/GRAPH.md) — including
254	the pre-curveball assumption, the Graph run that preceded the edit, and the test that pins the
255	preserved behaviour. Agent sessions run in this clone from now on are captured normally.
256	
257	The product also carries its own checkpoint layer (`entire-continuity checkpoint list`,
258	`task lineage`), which records the same milestones with intent, decisions and rejected approaches
259	attached — that is the thing being demonstrated, and it works against real Entire through
260	`internal/continuity/entire` whenever the binary answers.
261	
262	---
263	
264	## Setup, run and test instructions
265	
266	Requires Go 1.26+. No third-party dependencies — standard library only.
267	
268	```bash
269	go build ./...
270	go test ./...                     # 347 test functions across four layers
271	go build -o entire-continuity ./cmd/entire-continuity
272	```
273	
274	Try it against the curveball fixture — a format this build had never seen, from a runtime it had
275	never heard of:
276	
277	```bash
278	./entire-continuity ingest --file internal/normalize/testdata/lifecycle_v2_acmecode.jsonl
279	./entire-continuity task list
280	./entire-continuity task status <task-id>
281	./entire-continuity task handoff <task-id>
282	./entire-continuity task resume <task-id>
283	./entire-continuity task explain <task-id>
284	./entire-continuity graph impact Validate
285	```
286	
287	Or against the demo domain, where a task is deliberately unfinished:
288	
289	```bash
290	cd examples/billing && go test ./...     # TestDuplicateWebhook fails on purpose
291	cd ../.. && ./entire-continuity --repo examples/billing graph impact WebhookProcessor
292	```
293	
294	That last command is the §35 next-action validation: it names the callers, the components
295	downstream and the six tests to run after the change — *before* the edit, not after it.
296	
297	---
298	
299	## Known limitations and next steps
300	
301	Stated plainly, because a product whose thesis is "never present incomplete context as complete"
302	would be a poor advertisement for itself otherwise.
303	
304	- **Entire is installed and this work now lives in the Entire mirror clone** of `Yash-1706/external-agents` (India cluster, `aws-ap-south-1`), with checkpoints enabled and Entire Graph v0.4.0 active. The `EntireClient` port selects the real CLI automatically when the binary answers a probe, and falls back to a local store otherwise; every command prints which backend answered, and the fallback refuses to describe itself as Entire.
305	- **Entire Graph findings are from the real Graph** (v0.4.0); see [docs/GRAPH.md](docs/GRAPH.md). The local `go/ast` analyser still ships in `internal/continuity/graph` so the product degrades honestly where Graph is absent, but it is no longer what the evidence rests on — and notably it did *not* find the closed-set defect that Graph did.
306	- **OpenClaw and Hermes were not installed.** The hook shims in `adapters/` implement their
307	  documented surfaces, and `TestAdaptersFeedTheNormalizer` runs the real shims under Node and
308	  decodes what they actually wrote — but no shim has been driven by a live host process. Wiring
309	  one is a matter of registering it against that host's plugin API; the normalization layer it
310	  feeds would not change.
311	- **Semantic extraction is rule-based, not model-backed.** It sits behind `model.Extractor` so a
312	  model-backed implementation drops in unchanged. It deliberately **never** marks a requirement
313	  complete — a keyword rule has no basis to certify completion.
314	- `internal/model` has no direct unit tests; it is exercised through every package that uses it.
315	  `contextbuild` and `handoff` are covered by the end-to-end layer rather than by unit tests.
316	
317	**Next steps:** live hook shims driven by real OpenClaw and Hermes processes; a model-backed
318	extractor behind the existing `model.Extractor` port; multi-repository tasks.

1	# Entire Graph — findings and verification
2	
3	All output below is from **Entire Graph v0.4.0** (`entire plugin install graph`), run inside the
4	Entire mirror clone of `Yash-1706/external-agents`.
5	
6	An earlier version of this document recorded findings from a local `go/ast` fallback analyser,
7	used while Entire was not yet installed. Those are superseded by the real runs below. The fallback
8	still ships (`internal/continuity/graph`) because the product must degrade honestly when Graph is
9	absent — but it is no longer what this evidence rests on.
10	
11	---
12	
13	## 1. Definition lookup (`graph search`)
14	
15	```
16	$ entire graph search --query "detect transcript format per record and decode both formats" \
17	    --repo . --top-k 5 --format text
18	```
19	
20	```
21	CLOSED SET Format (const-group, 4 variants): adding a variant without adding an arm
22	  compiles and then falls out of the switch
23	  .../normalize/format.go:150 newDecoder 3/4 arms, default absent, checked at runtime
24	
25	1. .../normalize/format.go:193-215 score=38.2395 symbol=DetectFormat kind=function
26	   signals=path,body,symbol-name,graph:callers,complete-symbol
27	2. .../normalize/format.go:39-43   score=36.8280 symbol=Formats
28	3. .../cmd/entire-continuity/integration.go:231-237 symbol=formatList
29	```
30	
31	**This is the finding that changed the code.** Graph did not just locate the format logic — it
32	reported that `Format` is a closed set of 4 variants and that `newDecoder` covered 3 arms with no
33	`default`, so a future variant would compile and then fall out of the switch at runtime.
34	
35	Verifying it against source turned up a **live defect**, not just a latent one: `FormatAuto` is a
36	*valid* `Format`, but it reached the fallthrough and was reported as an **"unknown format"**. That
37	is a wrong answer to a caller who passed something legitimate — `auto` is not undecodable, it is
38	*unresolved*, and must be turned into a concrete format by `DetectFormat` first.
39	
40	Fixed in `a58128b`: the switch is now exhaustive with an explicit `FormatAuto` arm naming the real
41	mistake, plus `default`. `TestNewDecoderIsExhaustiveOverFormat` pins it, so a format added without
42	an arm fails a test instead of failing at runtime.
43	
44	Our own fallback analyser did **not** find this. Closed-set analysis over a const group is exactly
45	the structural reasoning a real code graph does and a name-resolving AST walk does not.
46	
47	---

81	than assumed to.

109	## What Graph changed, in one line
110	
111	> It found that a closed set of formats was matched non-exhaustively, which turned out to be
112	> misreporting a valid input as unknown — and it named the exact test that guards the behaviour we

1	# Noon Curveball — Track 3: The agent changed its format
2	
3	**Status:** implemented and tested.
4	**Pre-curveball baseline:** commit `e04266c` — the last stable state before any curveball edit.
5	**Graph impact analysis:** `2a6250b`, run *before* editing. See [GRAPH.md](GRAPH.md).
6	**Implementation:** `3f2ffa6`.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## 1. What the curveball requires
11	
12	> The agent or workflow you integrated has released a new transcript and lifecycle event format.
13	> Existing users still produce the original format.
14	
15	| # | Requirement | Where it lands |
16	|---|---|---|
17	| C1 | Support both the original and the new format | `internal/normalize` |
18	| C2 | Unknown events must not crash the integration | `internal/normalize`, `internal/model` event validation |
19	| C3 | An incomplete transcript must produce a **partial** result, not a corrupted or discarded session | `internal/normalize` → `internal/derive` → `Capture` |
20	| C4 | Existing Checkpoint behaviour must remain compatible | `internal/entire`, `EngineeringState` serialization |
21	| C5 | Tests for: original format, new format, unknown events, incomplete input | `internal/normalize/*_test.go` + fixtures |
22	| C6 | Do not duplicate the entire implementation for each format | architecture of `internal/normalize` |
23	
24	---
25	
26	## 2. The assumption the curveball invalidated
27	
28	The pre-curveball design encoded one assumption in three places:
29	
30	> **"Each host agent emits exactly one, stable, fully-enumerable lifecycle format. A normalizer is
31	> therefore a total function from raw envelope to known event, and anything it does not recognise
32	> is noise that can be discarded."**
33	
34	Concretely, that assumption is visible as:
35	
36	**A1 — One format per agent.**
37	`normalize.For(agent model.AgentKind) (Normalizer, error)` keys the parser off *agent identity
38	alone*. There is no format dimension anywhere in the signature, so there is no way to express
39	"OpenClaw, new format" versus "OpenClaw, original format".
40	
41	**A2 — Unrecognised records carry no information.**
42	The v1 rule was *skip unknown hook/event names silently*. That was defensible when the vocabulary
43	was closed: an unknown name meant a host feature we deliberately did not model. It is not
44	defensible once the host ships a new format, because then unknown names are exactly the records
45	that matter — and silently dropping them makes the timeline under-report while still *looking*
46	complete. That directly contradicts our own honesty rule (plan §33/§47): the product must never
47	present incomplete context as complete.
48	
49	**A3 — A transcript is either complete or invalid.**
50	`model.AgentEvent.Validate()` rejects a malformed record, and v1 normalize propagates that as an
51	error for the whole batch. One truncated trailing line in a JSONL transcript would therefore
52	discard an entire session's worth of recoverable events.
53	
54	The curveball breaks all three at once: **A1** because both formats are live simultaneously
55	("existing users still produce the original format"), **A2** because unknown events must be
56	survivable *and* visible, and **A3** because an incomplete transcript must still yield a usable
57	partial result.
58	
59	---
60	
61	## 3. How the design changes
62	
63	The fix is a **format dimension plus a declarative mapping table**, not a second parser.
64	
65	### 3.1 Formats become data, not code
66	
67	v1 had one hand-written decode path per agent. v2 introduces a `FormatSpec`: a declarative
68	description of an envelope — where the kind, timestamp, session, parent, role, task and payload
69	reference live, and a kind → `model.EventType` mapping table. One shared decode engine walks any
70	`FormatSpec`. Adding a format is adding a table, not a pipeline.
71	
72	This is what satisfies **C6**: the original and new formats share every line of decoding,
73	validation, redaction and lineage-folding logic. They differ only in their table.
74	
75	### 3.2 Format is detected, not assumed
76	
77	`normalize.For(agent, format)` gains the missing dimension, and `normalize.Detect(record)` sniffs
78	the envelope so a mixed stream — original and new records interleaved, which is exactly what a
79	partially-migrated fleet produces — decodes correctly record by record. An explicit override stays
80	available for when the caller knows better.
81	
82	### 3.3 Unknown events become first-class
83	
84	Unknown records are **retained**, not dropped: an event of type `Unknown` carrying its original
85	kind in `Attrs["raw_kind"]`. Nothing crashes (**C2**), and the fact that the timeline contains
86	records we could not interpret becomes *visible* rather than invisible.
87	
88	### 3.4 Partial input degrades into a partial result
89	
90	Decoding returns a `Report` — total, accepted, unknown, malformed, formats seen — which flows into
91	`Capture`. A truncated final line increments `malformed` and is skipped; the surrounding session
92	survives (**C3**). The renderer already has a `STATE PARTIALLY RECOVERED` path, and this feeds it
93	honest numbers.
94	
95	---
96	
97	## 4. Why the new result is safe
98	
99	This is the part that matters for "preserves existing behaviour":
100	
101	1. **The original format is pinned by golden tests written before the change.** Original-format
102	   fixtures must normalize byte-identically after the refactor. If they do not, the refactor is
103	   wrong, and the test says so.
104	
105	2. **The checkpoint writing path is untouched (C4).** `EngineeringState` keeps `schema_version: 1`;
106	   no field is removed or repurposed. A checkpoint written by v1 still loads, and a checkpoint
107	   written by v2 from original-format input is identical to the one v1 would have written.
108	
109	3. **The new information can only make output more cautious.** Unknown and malformed counts only
110	   ever *widen* `Capture.Missing`. Every downstream consumer treats a wider `Missing` as less
111	   certainty, never more. `validate.Enforce` is monotonically downgrading by construction — it
112	   cannot strengthen a claim — so no new code path can turn a partial transcript into a confident
113	   assertion.
114	
115	4. **The failure mode moved in the safe direction.** v1 could discard a whole session on one bad
116	   line (silent data loss that still rendered as a clean result). v2 keeps the session and reports
117	   the gap. The worst case changed from *confidently wrong* to *explicitly incomplete*.
118	
119	---
120	
121	## 5. Graph impact analysis
122	
123	> Run **before** editing. Findings recorded in [GRAPH.md](GRAPH.md).
124	
125	Target paths to enumerate with Graph impact analysis, per the curveball card — every parser,
126	lifecycle handler, summary path and checkpoint-writing path that consumes normalized events:
127	
128	- `normalize.Normalizer` implementations and their callers
129	- `model.AgentEvent.Validate` callers
130	- `model.EventType.Valid` callers
131	- `derive.State` (lifecycle → state)
132	- `store.AppendEvent` (lifecycle → lineage)
133	- `entire` checkpoint write path
134	- `render` summary paths that report capture completeness
135	
136	_This section is completed with real `graph impact` output before any code is edited._
137	
138	---
139	
140	## 6. What the real fixture changed
141	
142	The official JSONL fixture arrived after the analysis above was written, and it invalidated part
143	of it. Recording that rather than quietly editing the prediction, because the difference is the
144	point: the fixture broke *more* than the card's description implied.
145	
146	`internal/normalize/testdata/lifecycle_v2_acmecode.jsonl`, 17 records from a runtime calling
147	itself **AcmeCode 1.4.2**. Three properties were not predictable from the card:
148	
149	1. **It carries no `task_id` at all.** The predicted design assumed the new format would still
150	   name a task. It does not — it names a `repository`, a `branch` and a `session_id`. This is what
151	   turned the Graph finding about `Validate`'s three callers from interesting into decisive: an
152	   event with no task id fails validation at the boundary. The anchor is now *derived* through the
153	   existing `model.NewTaskID(repo, branch, session)`, which also makes ingestion idempotent — the
154	   same transcript always lands on the same task.
155	
156	2. **It names a runtime outside the enumerated vocabulary.** `AgentKind.Valid` rejected anything
157	   but the four constants, so every AcmeCode event would have failed validation. The closed agent
158	   vocabulary was part of the same invalidated assumption — *we can enumerate the world* — and was
159	   widened to accept any safe identifier. Two packages had already built private workarounds for
160	   this (`render` printed `Unknown (cursor)`, `entire` coerced to `unknown`); both are now
161	   redundant, which is the tell that the defect was in the model rather than in them.
162	
163	3. **It splits a tool call across two records** correlated by `call_id`. A test outcome is only
164	   knowable by remembering the call that produced it, so the decoder is stateful for the length of
165	   a stream. This is what lets the fixture's failing run (`exit_code 1`, "1 failed, 7 passed") and
166	   its later passing run (`exit_code 0`, "8 passed") resolve against each other under the §32 merge
167	   rule — a failing test stays failed until a *newer result for the same name* proves otherwise.
168	
169	The fixture also exercised two defects that had nothing to do with formats, found only because a
170	real transcript was run end to end:
171	
172	- The heuristic extractor mined rejection cues from **user prompts**, so the prompt "Coupons
173	  should be **rejected** if expired…" was recorded as a *rejected approach*. That tells the next
174	  worker not to build the very thing they were asked for — worse than extracting nothing. Cue
175	  mining is now restricted to agent-authored events.
176	- A task created by ingestion never recovered its **original intent**, the one field a later
177	  worker cannot reconstruct from the diff. It is now lifted from the checkpoint's stated intent,
178	  and the opening prompt is fed separately to requirement extraction, because the polished intent
179	  line and the prompt are different things and only the prompt carries the obligations.
180	
181	## 7. Verification
182	
183	```
184	go test ./...          # 323 test functions, all packages green
185	```
186	
187	The four cases the card requires each have a test in `internal/normalize/format_test.go`:
188	
189	| Case | Test |
190	|---|---|
191	| Original format | `TestOriginalFormatsStillDecode` — asserts the v1 fixtures decode **byte-identically** through the new path and the old one |
192	| New format | `TestLifecycleV2Fixture`, `TestLifecycleV2CorrelatesToolResults` |
193	| Unknown events | `TestUnknownEventsAreRetainedNotDropped`, `TestUnknownEventsInOriginalFormat` |
194	| Incomplete input | `TestIncompleteTranscriptProducesPartialResult`, `TestHeadlessTranscriptStillAnchors` |
195	
196	Plus `TestMixedFormatStream`, which decodes a single stream containing both formats at once.
197	
198	The first row is the one that matters for "preserves existing behaviour": it does not check that
199	the old fixtures still *work*, it checks that they produce exactly the same events they did
200	before, by running both paths and comparing.
201	
202	End to end, through the real CLI:
203	
204	```bash
205	entire-continuity ingest --file internal/normalize/testdata/lifecycle_v2_acmecode.jsonl
206	entire-continuity task status <task-id>
207	```
208	
209	recovers the intent, both test runs (resolved failing → passing by the merge rule), the
210	checkpoint, the session lineage and the runtime name — from a transcript in a format this build
211	had never seen, emitted by a runtime it had never heard of.

Graph results are evidence, not an oracle. Both findings above were verified against source before

---

## 4. A limitation, found by re-running the same query post-implementation

Re-running `graph impact` on `AgentEvent.Validate` after the curveball work landed — the same
symbol the §1 decisive finding was about — turned up a gap in Graph's own caller resolution.

```
$ entire graph impact --symbol AgentEvent.Validate --repo . --format text
```

```
Impact: AgentEvent.Validate (.../model/event.go:236) def=236 span=236-256 [method in AgentEvent]
Blast radius: 1 caller (1 direct, 0 transitive), 2 callees, 1 type consumer, 0 data flows,
              0 co-change files, 14 siblings.

Callers (1 direct, 0 transitive; who breaks if behavior changes):
- TestAgentEventValidate (.../model/model_test.go:172) [+2 more call sites]
```

Graph reports exactly **one caller, a test**. Grepping the source directly turns up production
callers Graph did not list:

- `.../derive/derive.go:243` — `ev.Validate()` where `ev model.AgentEvent`, inside a `for _, ev :=
  range in` loop
- `.../normalize/format.go:355`
- `.../normalize/normalize.go:234`
- `.../store/events.go:37`

That is the same shape of caller set the original design analysis in §1/§2 relied on (`normalize`,
`derive`, `store` — three packages). The live index is under-reporting it as one.

**Working hypothesis, not confirmed:** `Validate` is an overloaded method name — three distinct
types in this codebase define a method called `Validate` (`AgentEvent`, `Lineage`, and a
package-private `validate` function in a test fixture). The missed call sites are all on a
loop-variable value (`ev` from `for _, ev := range in`) rather than a directly-declared-type
reference, which is exactly the case where a resolver has to disambiguate an overloaded method by
inferred type instead of by literal declaration. That combination — overload plus loop-variable
receiver — is the most plausible reason the real callers dropped out of the CALLS edge set. This
was not root-caused inside Graph itself; it is a source-level observation about which call shapes
correlate with the miss.

**Why this matters for how we use Graph.** The whole product's evidence rule (`model.ConfidenceFor`)
says a claim with no evidence can never be better than `UNKNOWN`. The same rule applies to Graph
output about the repository itself: an impact result is evidence to verify, not a ground truth to
forward uncritically. Concretely, this means:

- Never present `graph impact` caller counts to a next-worker as a completeness guarantee ("only 1
  caller" must not be read as "safe to change with no other blast radius") — cross-check with a
  grep for the symbol name before treating a low caller count as license to skip validation.
- The §2 impact-analysis-before-a-high-risk-change step should not stop at the tool's caller list
  when the symbol name is a common one (`Validate`, `Run`, `Handle`, etc.) likely to be overloaded
  across types — that is precisely the condition under which this gap appeared.
- This does not retract the §1 finding. The `FormatAuto` closed-set defect was found by a different
  analysis (const-group exhaustiveness over `DetectFormat`'s switch), not by caller counting, and
  remains verified against source. The two findings are independent; only the caller-count query
  is now known to be unreliable for overloaded method names on loop-variable receivers.

No fix is proposed here beyond the workaround above (grep alongside `graph impact` for common
method names) — this is Graph's own resolver, not this repository's code, so there is nothing in
this codebase to patch. Recording it is the honest-degradation rule (plan §33/§47) applied to the
tool itself, not just to transcript capture.
